newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson sues to block Great Western defenses.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson sues to block Great Western defenses.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson and Co, which Tuesday proposed an unsolicited $6 billion merger with Great Western Financial Corp, has sued Great Western and its directors in a legal preemptive strike intended to dismantle Great Western's defensive measures against hostile takeovers.
In papers filed Tuesday in the Delaware Chancery Court, Ahmanson said it expects Great Western to use its poison pill and Delaware anti-takeover law to try to block the merger.
"The GWF (Great Western Financial) board should not be allowed to deprive stockholders of GWF the opportunity to decide upon the merits of the proposed merger for themselves," court papers said.
Ahmanson said further that the use of any defensive measure would be "an unreasonable response to the proposed merger in violation of the fiduciary duties" of Great Western's officers and directors.

Under the Ahmanson proposal, each outstanding share of Great Western would be converted into 1.05 shares of Ahmanson common stock with a value of $42.53, a 24 percent premium over the closing price of Great Western common on Friday.
Ahmanson says the proposed merger would be tax-free, non-coercive and non-discriminatory.

Ahmanson said that at the next annual meeting of Great Western it would nominate its slate for three class II director seats. The proxy fight is part of Ahmanson's plan to prevent the board from applying defensive measures against the Ahmanson proposal.

Ahmanson said in court papers that it is the beneficial owner of 100 shares of Great Western. Should Ahmanson increase its holdings to 15 percent of outstanding stock, that would trigger Great Western's rights plan or poison pill, allowing its shareholders to buy its stock at half the market price and making a merger prohibitively expensive.
Ahmanson said it believes "the GWF board does not intend to redeem the rights to accomodate the proposed merger or the proxy solicitation."
At the 15 percent ownership level, Delaware's anti-takeover law would also be activated.
Under the law, a business combination or merger would be prohibited for three years unless one of three conditions were met.

The merger would have to be pre-approved by the target company's board; the interested stockholder would have to acquire 85 percent of the stock when it crossed the 15 percent threshold; or the board and two-thirds of the non-acquiring shareholders would have to approve the merger after the 15 percent threshold were reached.

In its lawsuit, Ahmanson has asked for a court order requiring Great Western not to apply the poison pill against the proposed merger and to approve the merger so that the Delaware anti-takeover law would not take effect.
Ahmanson also seeks a court declaration that any defensive action against the merger by the directors would be a breach of their fiduciary duty.
Great Western spokesman Charles Coleman told Reuters the company did not have a comment about the lawsuit at this time.
